extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of political theory and public administration (comparative government)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing how democratic institutions affect administration, public finance, and the conduct of public officers, with guidance on comparing expenditures across polities. Draws on comparative observation (primarily United States vs France) to identify causal tendencies and measurement difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of official discretion / magistrate independence
rubrics_metrics.description: In democratic republics much is left by the law to the arbitrary determination of the magistrate; American functionaries are much more independent in the sphere the law traces out for them than public officers in Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This independence often means the object is pointed out and the means are left to the officer's discretion (examples: New England selectmen drawing jury lists, posting habitual drunkards). Independence suits democracies but requires safeguards to prevent encroachment on authority and liberties; excessive arbitrary power would be intolerable in other regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of legal supervision over public officers
rubrics_metrics.description: In limited monarchies the law prescribes the sphere in which public officers are to act and superintends their measures; King and people share interest in magistrate stability and therefore agree to restrict officers to conduct laid down beforehand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where power is divided (King vs people) both parties have incentives to render officers independent while simultaneously instituting securities to prevent abuse. Assess whether the legal framework both confines officials and prevents evasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instability of administration (tenure, record-keeping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public acts in America frequently leave fewer traces than private occurrences; public administration is often oral and traditionary with little committed to writing and archives not formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instability and short terms of officials impede the formation of archives and the transmission of administrative knowledge, harming the development of administration as a science. Good administration requires written records, methodical systems, and continuity so successive administrators can build on predecessors' discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of democracy to national culture and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy always presupposes the existence of a high degree of culture and enlightenment in society and is better adapted to people already versed in administration than to a nation uninitiated in public affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the populace has sufficient civic knowledge and experience to exercise democratic governance successfully; democracies imposed on politically uninitiated societies risk poor administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency of public expenditure under democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Public expenditure tends to increase when the people governs; democratic republics generally have more considerable public expenditure than absolute monarchies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include that majorities who legislate are often not themselves bearing the taxes and thus favor spending benefiting them; also democratic impatience for improvements and innovations produces many costly undertakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of class composition on fiscal policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Communities divide into three classes (wealthy, middling, poor), and each class's control of legislation affects public finances: wealthy rule -> less public spending; middle-class rule -> most economical; poor-majority rule -> expenditure increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the poor (relative sense) possess legislative power they tend to levy taxes in ways that are burdensome to the wealthy and advantageous to themselves, producing higher expenditures. Assess which socio-economic class dominates lawmaking to predict fiscal tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderating effect of property distribution on democratic extravagance
rubrics_metrics.description: The extravagance of democracy is less to be feared as the people acquires a share of property; universal suffrage is less dangerous where the majority possess some fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the majority own property, they are less likely to favor fiscally extravagant measures that would harm their own interests. Consider property distribution when judging democratic fiscal behavior (example: America vs France).

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic propensity for costly innovations and reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic communities are agitated by an ill-defined excitement and impatience that engenders a multitude of innovations, almost all attended with expense; the rulers seek perpetual ameliorations because they feel the people's miseries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect numerous reform proposals and public projects in democracies; evaluate administrative capacity to execute and complete undertakings (unfinished or poorly conducted projects waste funds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary structure tendencies under democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracies tend to economize on salaries of principal officers while paying subordinate officers relatively well — the secondary officers are placed in easy circumstances, the dignitaries worse than elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This results from popular notions of fairness (public servants should be placed similarly to the public) and envy toward higher officials. When assessing remuneration policy, consider popular perceptions and the potential impact on recruitment and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative fiscal analysis prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate and compare public charges two preliminaries are indispensable: knowledge of (1) the national wealth, and (2) the portion of that wealth devoted to State expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without knowing both total resources and the share consumed by the State, comparisons of expenditure are misleading. Analysts must attempt to measure population, real property, and personal property and to compute the proportion devoted to public charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements composing national wealth for fiscal comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The wealth of nations is composed of three elements: population, real property, and personal property; population is easiest to measure, the other two are difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate comparison of taxation requires attempts to quantify all three elements; shortcomings in measuring land values and personal property make international fiscal comparisons problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical indicators when statistical data are lacking
rubrics_metrics.description: In absence of positive documents, form an opinion on taxation burden from signs: whether external appearance is flourishing; whether after taxes the poor retain subsistence and the rich enjoyment; whether industry lacks capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visible socio-economic signs to infer the relation of taxation to prosperity when precise statistics are unavailable; these qualitative indicators can suggest whether citizens contribute a large or small portion of income to the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of non-monetary contributions in assessing public burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments demand not only money but personal services (e.g., army, militia) which are equivalent to a given sum and should be considered when comparing burdens across countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count time and services conscripted by the State as part of citizens' contributions; failure to include these leads to underestimation of total burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for institutional differences in types of public obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences such as paying clergy vs voluntary support, legal provision for the poor vs charity, fixed salaries vs perquisites, and turnpikes vs free roads all affect comparability of public expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing countries, adjust for structural differences in who bears costs and how services are provided; otherwise expenditure comparisons are misleading (examples contrasting France and America).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity from multiple budgetary layers and municipal variation
rubrics_metrics.description: In federations like the United States there are multiple budgets (Union, States, Counties, Townships) and municipal responsibilities differ between polities, complicating calculation of total public expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fair comparison must aggregate across all relevant budgets and account for differing allocations of municipal functions; inability to obtain smaller-unit budgets (e.g., townships) undermines accurate totals.
